title: No One Carries Everyone
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 5 of 40
content:
Katara was very good at noticing when everyone else needed rest.

She was terrible at noticing when she did.

The clinic stayed open three hours past sunset because a boiler explosion on the south side sent twelve injured workers through the doors. None of the wounds were life-threatening. That did not mean they were easy. Burns hurt. Fear hurt. A man who thought he might lose the use of his hand cried into his wife’s shoulder while Katara knelt beside him and told him exactly what she could heal and exactly what would take time.

I spent the evening carrying water, recording names, and keeping frightened relatives from blocking the treatment tables.

Aang arrived twice and was sent away twice.

The first time Katara told him she was busy.

The second time I told him she would murder him if he tried to be helpful by reorganizing supplies.

“She likes when I help.”

“She likes when you help correctly.”

He considered this.

“Fair.”

Toph arrived around midnight with food.

“Eat,” she ordered.

Katara did not look up. “In a minute.”

Toph set the bowl directly on Katara’s patient ledger.

“Now.”

“I am literally writing.”

“Not anymore.”

Katara’s eyes flashed.

Toph crossed her arms.

I stepped between them with the confidence of a person who had temporarily misplaced survival instinct.

“I’ll finish the ledger.”

Katara looked at me. “You don’t know the treatment notes.”

“You tell me. I write. Revolutionary system.”

Her mouth tightened.

That was when I saw her hand shake.

Only once.

Fatigue, not fear.

I took the pen.

“Katara.”

She looked at me.

No title. No teasing. No argument.

“Sit down.”

For one long second I thought she would refuse purely because I had used her own command against her.

Then Toph snorted.

Katara sank onto the bench.

“Traitors,” she muttered.

Toph shoved the bowl into her hands. “You love us.”

Katara looked at the stew.

Something in her face softened.

“That’s the problem.”

Toph went still.

I sat beside Katara while she ate.

The last patient left after one in the morning. Aang returned with blankets and did not attempt to reorganize anything. He simply moved through the room extinguishing lamps while Katara checked each bed one final time.

“You can go home,” she told the remaining healer.

The healer gave her a flat look. “So can you.”

Toph made an approving sound.

Katara ignored all of us.

Outside, rain had begun.

Aang opened an umbrella. Toph refused to stand under it because the handle was metal and she claimed she could bend it into a better umbrella if necessary.

Katara walked two blocks before her pace slowed.

I fell into step beside her.

“You’re limping,” I said.

“I’m tired.”

“You’re limping because you’re tired.”

“I know how legs work.”

“Debatable.”

She gave me a look.

Then she laughed.

It was small and exhausted.

Aang and Toph had moved ahead, arguing about whether Appa could fit on the clinic roof.

Katara glanced at them.

“They worry.”

“So do you.”

“I’m better at it.”

“No. You’re louder.”

She bumped my shoulder.

Rain tapped the umbrella Aang had forced into my hand before running ahead.

After another block, Katara said, “My mother died because she protected me.”

The sentence came without warning.

I did not answer too quickly.

Katara watched the wet street ahead.

“I know that’s not why I do this,” she continued. “I know people like to make everything about one wound. I’m not that simple.”

“No.”

“But sometimes…” Her fingers tightened around the strap of her medical bag. “Sometimes if someone is hurting and I could help, leaving feels like choosing not to be there.”

I understood then that her care had teeth.

People saw warmth first. They saw healing water, speeches, hope. They did not always see the fear beneath it: the child who had lost someone because danger came and there had been nothing she could do.

“You can’t be everywhere,” I said.

“I know.”

“You can’t save everyone.”

“I know.”

“And knowing doesn’t make it feel better.”

Her eyes turned toward me.

“No.”

We stopped beneath the awning of a closed shop.

Aang and Toph had noticed and were waiting farther down the street.

Katara’s face was pale with fatigue.

I lifted one hand, slowly enough to give her time to move away, and touched her cheek.

She leaned into my palm.

The gesture was so immediate that my chest tightened.

“You don’t have to earn rest,” I said.

Katara closed her eyes.

For several breaths, rain filled the silence.

When she opened them again, something had changed.

Her gaze dropped to my mouth.

Mine dropped to hers.

Neither of us moved closer.

Not yet.

Katara smiled faintly. “You’re very bossy for someone who accused me of being bossy.”

“I learned from an expert.”

“That sounds like flirting.”

“It might be.”

Her smile became real.

Aang called from down the street, “Do we need to walk slower?”

Toph shouted, “Their heartbeats say yes!”

Katara groaned.

I laughed into my hand.

“Someday,” Katara said, “I am going to freeze Toph’s feet to the ground.”

“She’ll bend the ground.”

“I know. That’s why I haven’t bothered.”

We caught up with them.

Aang looked from Katara to me and smiled in a way that was far too knowing.

Toph did not say anything.

That was worse.

At their house, Katara tried to insist I did not need to stay.

Aang ignored her and made tea.

Toph claimed the couch.

I found blankets.

Katara stood in the middle of the room looking offended by the conspiracy.

“No,” Aang said gently.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were about to.”

“I was going to say I’m fine.”

Toph threw a cushion at her.

Katara caught it without looking.

Aang walked over and kissed her forehead.

The tenderness between them did not make me feel excluded.

That surprised me.

It made the room feel safer.

Katara looked at me over Aang’s shoulder.

There was a question in her expression.

I did not know the answer yet.

I only knew I wanted to stay long enough to find it.

We ended up on the floor around the low table, drinking tea too late at night. Toph leaned against one side of the couch, feet planted. Aang rested his head in Katara’s lap. Katara’s shoulder touched mine.

No one made a declaration.

No one needed to.

For that one quiet hour, care moved in every direction.

Aang refilled Katara’s cup.

Katara tucked a blanket over Toph’s legs while pretending she had not.

Toph kicked a cushion under my back when she noticed me shifting.

I wrote down the clinic’s final totals so Katara would not wake up worrying about them.

No one carried everyone.

That was the point.

We carried what we could, and when our arms got tired, someone else reached for the weight.

I had never known love could begin to look like that before anyone had even called it love.

Katara did sleep eventually.

Not because any of us convinced her she deserved it. That argument only made her more stubborn. Instead, Toph sat directly in the clinic doorway and announced that nobody was allowed to bring Katara another problem unless the building was actively on fire.

“What if somebody is bleeding?” a volunteer asked.

“Is it a lot?”

“Toph.” Katara’s warning voice could still cut stone when she was exhausted.

I took the volunteer’s clipboard. “I’ve got it.”

Aang collected the next one. “Me too.”

Katara looked between us. “You don’t know the supply system.”

“Then teach us tomorrow,” I said.

Her jaw tightened.

For one second I thought she would fight.

Then the fight left her shoulders all at once.

That frightened me more than the argument would have.

Aang saw it too. He did not reach for her immediately. He simply moved the spare blanket from the shelf to the narrow cot in the back room.

“You can close the curtain,” he said. “We’ll wake you if there’s an emergency.”

“And define emergency correctly,” Katara muttered.

Toph raised a hand. “Fire larger than me.”

“No.”

“Fine. Larger than Aang.”

“No.”

Katara was smiling despite herself when she disappeared behind the curtain.

An hour later, a child arrived with a split lip and a terrified father. I cleaned the cut while Aang distracted the child by making a scrap of gauze dance in tiny circles. Toph found the missing registration ledger by feeling the cabinet hinges vibrate when I slammed the wrong drawer.

None of us did Katara’s job as well as Katara.

That was never the point.

When she woke, the clinic was still standing. People had been helped. The world had continued without requiring her to hold every edge together.

She stared at the three of us.

“Do not look smug.”

Toph looked extraordinarily smug.

When Katara returned to work the next day, she found the clinic ledger reorganized, badly labeled, and completely usable.

She stared at it.

Toph said, “You’re welcome.”

Katara laughed until she had to sit down.

The next evening, after the clinic had finally settled, I stayed behind with Katara to finish the medicine inventory. She counted bandages. I counted the number of times she'd forgotten to eat.

“There's something I need to say,” I told her. “Before feelings turn into plans that nobody actually agreed to.”

She set down the ledger.

“I practice ethical non-monogamy, and I prefer polyamory. I care about you. I also care about Aang and Toph. I'm not asking you to make one decision for all three of you.”

Katara looked at me for a long moment. “Thank you for saying it to me, not through Aang.”

“You're your own person.”

“Exactly.” She tapped the ledger. “And if this becomes a relationship, I need us to talk about time, jealousy, and what happens when public duties pull us in different directions. Caring isn't enough if nobody knows where anyone stands.”

“I agree.”

“Good,” she said, with a tired half-smile. “Now hand me that list before I become sentimental.”

I found Aang in the courtyard the following morning, helping a child repair a paper kite. When the child ran away, I told him the same truth in my own words: ethical non-monogamy, polyamory by preference, and honest consent before either of us assumed an answer.

Aang rubbed the back of his neck. “I think I understand the idea. I don't know if I understand all the feelings yet.”

“Neither do I. Not in advance.”

He laughed, relieved. “Then maybe we learn without pretending we're experts.”

“We also ask Katara and Toph what they want. Separately.”

“Separately,” he agreed, and his seriousness mattered more than the smile.

Toph cornered me by the academy stairs that afternoon.

“You've been walking around like a person about to make a speech.”

“I have something to tell you.”

“Then tell me.”

“I practice ethical non-monogamy. I prefer polyamory. It isn't a game and it isn't a way around commitment. If there's something between us, I want you to know that.”

She crossed her arms. “You think I want to get folded into somebody else's relationship just because we all happen to like the same idiot?”

“No. That's why I'm telling you.”

“Good.” She leaned close enough for me to hear the grin in her voice. “I want my own dates, my own arguments, and a say in every rule that concerns me. Also, nobody gets to call this a cute arrangement.”

“Noted. The arrangement is deeply intimidating.”

“Better.”

She nudged my shoe with hers, then went back to work.

None of the conversations settled our future. Each made room for a future none of us would have to guess our way into.
